Alright, I've just finished laying down the core REST API in server/api.js. That file defines the authentication routes, user profile handling, catalog fetching, game creation, and various game‑related actions. It also sets up some constants like MAX_PARTS and the allowed part types, which will be useful later for validation. The next major piece of the platform is the real‑time component: users need to be able to join multiplayer lobbies, see each other’s avatars, and collaborate in the studio editor. All of that will be driven over WebSockets, since the HTTP API is only for request/response and can't push updates.

Before I jump into writing the WebSocket hub, I should double‑check what I've already scaffolded. The directory structure under /home/lane/rblx currently looks like this:

- server/
  - db.js (tiny JSON persistence)
  - catalog.js (item definitions)
  - seed.js (procedural default games)
  - api.js (REST endpoints)
- public/
  - vendor/three.module.js (client‑side 3D engine)
  - css/, js/engine/, js/studio/ (placeholders for client code)
- data/ (will hold db.json)

I have the express server ready to serve static files and the API routes, but I haven’t yet instantiated the WebSocket server. I also need a place to keep track of active lobby state (players, their positions, current game mode, etc.) and a way for the studio client to broadcast part edits to all collaborators in the same game session. The db layer already provides a simple in‑memory object with a `sessions` map, which I can repurpose to store live lobby data temporarily (it will be cleared on server restart, which is acceptable for this prototype).

Given this, the logical next step is to create a new module—maybe call it `realtime.js` or `hub.js`—that sets up a ws.Server attached to the existing Express HTTP server. This hub will handle connection upgrades, authenticate users via the same token mechanism used in the REST API, and then join them to a lobby based on a game ID. It will need to emit events like `playerJoined`, `playerLeft`, `stateUpdate`, and `studioEdit`. On the client side, the engine and studio scripts will open a WebSocket to this endpoint and listen for those events.

Since the user explicitly asked for “multiplayer lobbies with REAL players/connections” and “full collaboration with other users” in the studio, the hub must support both gameplay and editing channels. I can design a simple protocol where each message has a `type` field (`join`, `move`, `edit`, `chat`, etc.) and a `payload`. For now, I’ll just scaffold the hub with connection handling, basic authentication, and placeholders for the lobby logic. I’ll also export the hub so the main server entry point can require it and start it after the Express app is set up.

Thus, the next thing to communicate to the user is that I'm moving on to the real‑time hub implementation, which will cover play lobbies and studio collaboration over WebSocket. This keeps the narrative clear and shows progress toward the required features.Now realtime hub — play lobbies + studio collab over WebSocket.
